text: ISO 27001 gets lumped together with SOC 2 constantly, as if they're two flavors of the same thing. They're not. SOC 2 is a report describing what an auditor found. ISO 27001 is a certification of something much bigger — an entire management system for handling information security risk, issued by an accredited certification body after real external review.

That's the core difference worth holding onto: a SOC 2 report describes controls at a point in time or across a review window. An ISO 27001 certificate asserts that a whole system — risk assessment feeding decisions, decisions feeding controls, controls being monitored, monitoring feeding the next risk cycle — is actually in place and running. That system is called the ISMS, and it's the real thing being certified.

People new to ISO 27001 usually assume it's about which specific controls you've checked off. It isn't, mainly. The standard's clauses require a defined scope, management commitment, a documented risk methodology, defined roles, and a running Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle of internal audits and management review. The certification is really asking whether a functioning system exists underneath all of this, not just a one-time push.

Annex A supplies a catalog of controls — 93 of them across four themes — but it's not a mandatory checklist. The document that makes an organization's actual selection auditable is the Statement of Applicability: for every Annex A control, it records whether it's applicable, how it's implemented if so, and a documented justification if it's excluded. A vague or missing justification for an exclusion is a legitimate red flag in due diligence.

And certification isn't a one-time event. A Stage 1 audit reviews documentation and readiness, a Stage 2 audit tests whether the ISMS is actually implemented, and that's when certification is granted if successful. After that, annual surveillance audits confirm the ISMS is still functioning, and a full recertification audit happens roughly every three years — so losing the thread shows up quickly, not three years later.

That's ISO 27001 in practice: a certified management system, backed by an SoA that's more revealing than the certificate itself. Next lesson turns to PCI DSS and HIPAA — regulation that applies only when a specific kind of data, payment cards or health information, is actually in scope, not something an organization opts into the way it does with SOC 2 or ISO 27001.
